unitDescription.value: In this five-week intensive unit, students develop practical 3D modelling skills using SketchUp. Through a sequence of guided activities and short design challenges, they learn to create accurate geometric forms, use dimensions and scale, organise models with groups and components, apply materials, and present designs using scenes and appropriate views. The unit focuses on building confidence, precision and efficient modelling practices while demonstrating how digital models can be used to explore, communicate and refine design ideas. Rather than completing a formal assessment, students produce a collection of increasingly complex models that prepare them to use 3D visualisation and computer-aided design in future design projects.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students begin by orienting themselves to the SketchUp workspace, focusing on viewport navigation using the orbit, pan, and zoom tools. Lesson time is dedicated to mastering the 3D axis system and learning to place geometric primitives with precise numerical input. Students participate in scaffolded exercises that require them to draw shapes to specific dimensions, reinforcing the connection between 2D sketches and 3D volume.

resources.value: SketchUp for Web, lab workstations, mouse with scroll wheel, digital 'Quick Start' reference guide, dimensioned worksheet templates.

theory.value: The theory focuses on the Cartesian coordinate system as the foundation for all 3D modelling. Students examine how SketchUp uses three axes (X, Y, Z) to define spatial depth and orientation. Concepts of scale, absolute vs relative dimensions, and the importance of working at a 1:1 scale are explicitly taught to ensure models are accurate for real-world application. Students also learn about the 'sticky' nature of geometry, where raw edges and faces automatically merge if not managed through logical grouping.

prac.value: Practical tasks involve the creation of basic primitives such as cubes, cylinders, and prisms using the Line, Rectangle, and Circle tools. Students refine these shapes using the Push/Pull tool to generate 3D forms. They practice 'inferencing'—utilising the software’s internal snap points to align objects precisely along axes, ensuring no gaps or stray geometry remain in their initial constructions.

assessment.value: Formative: Teacher observation of modelling accuracy and workflow during initial primitive construction tasks.

outlineTheme.value: Students are introduced to the SketchUp interface and foundational 3D modelling concepts, including the 3D axis system and navigation tools. Through guided tutorials, they learn to construct basic geometric primitives using precision input for dimensions, establishing the importance of accurate modelling from the outset.

activities.title: We Do: Co-constructing a Dimensioned Cylinder

Next, demonstrate the Push/Pull extrusion: 'Activate Push/Pull by pressing P, hover over the circular face until it highlights with dots, push upward along the blue Z-axis, type 2000, and press Enter.' keyTeachingExperiences.value: Building on foundational shapes, students engage in lessons dedicated to more complex transformation techniques. They explore how to sweep profiles along paths using the Follow Me tool and replicate geometry efficiently using the Array command. Lessons integrate critical thinking as students choose the most efficient modelling strategy to recreate specific functional objects, such as a table leg or a profile-based container.

theory.value: Explicit teaching centres on 'Procedural Modelling'—the practice of using transformation tools to minimise manual effort. Students discuss the critical distinction between raw geometry and Components, examining how components allow for singular updates to multiple identical objects, thus enhancing model efficiency. The concept of 'geometric hierarchy' is introduced, teaching students to encapsulate distinct parts of a model into named groups to maintain structural integrity and prevent unexpected surface merging.

prac.value: Students undertake a sequence of modelling tasks that require the application of the Offset, Follow Me, and Rotate-plus-Copy (Array) tools. They create a functional assembly, such as a simple chair or a mechanical bracket, ensuring each component is correctly grouped and placed. A significant portion of time is spent debugging models where students have neglected to use groups, necessitating the re-isolation of geometry to achieve a 'manifold' (water-tight) mesh.

activities.title: Modelling Arrays and Rotation
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the Rotate-plus-Copy tool in SketchUp. Model the exact sequence: select a grouped component, activate the Rotate tool (Q), tap Ctrl to toggle copy mode, set the centre pivot point, establish the baseline reference angle, rotate 60 degrees, and immediately enter 'x6' in the Measurements box. Explicitly demonstrate the failure state where ungrouped raw geometry merges and distorts ('sticky geometry'), explaining how component encapsulation prevents mesh corruption.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the live demonstration on the projector screen, record the modifier shortcuts in the workbook table, and observe how component encapsulation isolates geometry prior to transformation.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the transformation reference table in your workbook as the Rotate-plus-Copy array sequence is demonstrated.
activities.questioning:
Why is it critical to group or convert an object into a component before applying an array? Expected: To prevent newly generated geometry from merging with or sticking to existing surfaces, maintaining a clean and manageable model mesh.
What keyboard modifier toggles copy mode when using the Rotate tool in SketchUp? Expected: The Control key (Ctrl on Windows / Option on macOS), which displays a plus icon beside the protractor cursor.
How do you specify six equally spaced copies after entering the initial rotation angle? Expected: Type 'x6' (or '*6') immediately after placing the copy and press Enter.
activities.scaffolding:
Procedural steps for radial array in SketchUp:
1. Select geometry and convert to Component (Right-click > Make Component).
2. Activate Rotate tool (Q).
3. Tap Ctrl to toggle Copy mode (cursor shows + symbol).
4. Click pivot centre point, then click baseline start edge.
5. Rotate to desired angle and click.
6. Type multiplier (e.g. *6 or x6) and press Enter.

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce core vocabulary for sweeping operations: Profile, Path, Sweep, and Perpendicular Alignment. Model the technical definition of each on the whiteboard. Why must the profile face be perpendicular to the starting edge of the path? Expected: To prevent distortion, self-intersection, or shearing of the swept 3D cross-section.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Profile: A closed 2D face that defines the cross-sectional shape of the extruded volume.
- Path: A continuous line, arc, or series of connected edges that directs the trajectory of the sweep.
- Sweep: The procedural transformation of generating a 3D solid by driving a 2D profile along a path.
- Perpendicularity: Maintaining a 90-degree alignment between the profile plane and the initial path vector.

activities.title: Camera Optics: Perspective versus Parallel Projection
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the mathematical and visual distinction between Perspective and Parallel Projection in SketchUp. Switch the camera via Camera > Parallel Projection and select Camera > Standard Views > Front. Explicitly demonstrate: 'In Parallel Projection, projection lines never converge; parallel edges remain strictly parallel. This is mandatory for technical elevations and manufacturing drawings because dimensions can be scaled directly. In Perspective, lines converge toward vanishing points, mimicking human eyesight.' Demonstrate adjusting Field of View (FOV) by selecting the Zoom tool and typing '35 deg' versus '75 deg' to show how wide angles distort architectural edges and create 'fish-eye' effects.

expected: It introduces exaggerated barrel distortion and perspective foreshortening, making edges appear warped and stretched, which misrepresents the true dimensions of the model.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Camera Concepts:
- Parallel Projection: Orthogonal viewing mode where projection rays are parallel; critical for 2D plans, technical elevations, and dimensioning.
- Perspective: Viewing mode where lines converge at vanishing points; communicates the human eye experience and provides spatial context.
- Field of View (FOV): The angular extent of the observable world seen through the camera lens (standard architectural default is 35 degrees).

activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the scene configuration protocol. 'Students, focus on the distinction between orthographic and perspective views. Select Standard View. 3. Open Scene Manager, click the plus icon, and rename exactly (e.g., '01_Front_Elevation'). For your Isometric render, switch back to Perspective, toggle Shadows, and ensure the Field of View is a professional 45 degrees. If you adjust your view, right-click the scene tab and select Update immediately. This ensures your final export matches your saved state.'

activities.title: Vocabulary: Professional Modelling Standards
activities.teacherDoes: Direct students to the vocabulary matching table in their workbooks. Explicitly define technical terms: 'geometric accuracy' (precision of dimensions relative to origin), 'component hierarchy' (parent-child grouping in Outliner), 'clean geometry' (absence of stray lines or overlapping faces), and 'workflow efficiency' (economy of tool usage and minimal redundant steps). Model how to cross-reference terms in the bank with the locked rows.

activities.questioning:
Why is maintaining a clean component hierarchy critical for complex assemblies? Expected: It prevents accidental geometry merging and allows rapid editing of recurring parts across the entire assembly.
How does geometric accuracy directly impact the rendering and presentation phase? Expected: Accurate geometry ensures proper shadow alignment, eliminates light leaks through unjoined faces, and guarantees realistic visual output.
activities.scaffolding:
Full Vocabulary Definitions:
- Geometric Accuracy: Precision of numerical dimensions and alignment relative to model origin.
- Component Hierarchy: Structured parent-child organisation of grouped parts within the Outliner.
- Clean Geometry: Absence of stray lines, overlapping faces, or unassigned materials.
- Workflow Efficiency: Economy of tool usage and minimal redundant steps to achieve required modelling outcomes.
